q: Neither gritty nor sticky, workable in spring and still holding something back in July, because sand, silt and clay are all present in useful proportion. What is that mixture called?
exp: Loam names a balance of particle sizes rather than a rock, and most of the world's farmland is a loam of one kind or another. For wine it is often too good: deep loam grows a very large vine, so a grower on it spends the year restraining growth rather than encouraging it.

q: Rub three damp soils between finger and thumb: one grates, one feels like flour and one smears into a skin. Ranked from the coarsest particle to the finest, what is the order?
exp: The three words are strict size classes rather than impressions: a sand grain can be seen with the naked eye, a silt particle cannot, and a clay particle is smaller again by a wide margin. Nearly everything a soil does with water follows from where it sits in that ranking.

q: The same rain falls on a sandy block and a clay block; one is dry by the following morning and the other is still wet a fortnight later. Which difference accounts for that?
opts: The size of the pores between particles, since wide channels drain and fine ones hold
The depth to which each of the two blocks was ploughed before planting
The number of vines planted in each, since more roots draw more water
The colour of the two soils, since one absorbs far more of the day's sunlight
exp: Gravity pulls water easily out of large pores and cannot pull it out of very fine ones, where surface tension holds it in place. That single piece of physics sits behind almost every practical claim made about soil in a vineyard.

q: White, soft enough to scratch with a fingernail, and built almost entirely from the skeletons of microscopic sea creatures. Which rock is that?
exp: Chalk is an unusually pure and unusually soft limestone, soft enough that a hammer turns it to powder rather than chipping it. It is also full of fine pores, so it takes water up like a blotter and hands it back slowly, which is why a thin soil over chalk can still carry a vine through a rainless August.

q: A few drops of dilute acid on a soil sample make it fizz. What has that told you?
opts: The soil is calcareous, which is to say rich in lime
The soil carries an unusually large quantity of iron
The soil was formed from volcanic ash rather than from sediment
The soil is acidic, and lime will have to be added to it
exp: The fizz is carbon dioxide coming off calcium carbonate, so the ground is limestone-derived and alkaline. It is the quickest field test there is, and it is the difference between planting on the assumption of lime and planting on the knowledge of it.

q: Ploughing turns up small fossil shells across a vineyard in northern France, and the pale rock they came out of breaks easily in the hand. What does that say about the ground?
opts: It is glacial rubble, scraped off a coastline a long way away
It is limestone, formed on the floor of a shallow sea
It is volcanic, and the shells were carried in on falling ash
It is a river deposit, and the shells were washed down from upstream
exp: Most limestone is compacted marine debris, which is why fossils fall out of it and why so much of Europe's white wine grows on ground that used to be a seabed. The shells are the best evidence a field can hand you, since neither falling ash nor river gravel nor glacial rubble arrives with sea creatures in it.

q: Roots push straight into one limestone and can only follow the cracks in another. Which property separates the two?
opts: The depth of soil lying over it, since that is what softens the rock beneath
How much iron the rock holds, since iron is what binds a limestone together
How hard the rock is, since a soft chalky one gives way and a hard one does not
The colour of the rock, since a darker stone warms and weathers much faster
exp: Soft chalk crumbles under a root, while a hard grey limestone has to be worked around through joints and fissures. Both can carry a vine through a dry summer, but the hard rock manages it only where it is well fractured, which is why one limestone slope can be excellent and the next one useless.

q: A dark fine-grained rock that splits into flat plates, and lies in loose broken sheets down the steepest slopes of northern Europe. Which rock is it?
exp: Slate cleaves along parallel planes, which is why it roofs houses and why a slate vineyard is a slope of tilted plates rather than of earth. It weathers slowly, so the soil over it is always thin.

q: Every heavy storm carries soil to the bottom of a steep slate vineyard, and the crew spends days afterwards carrying it back up in baskets. What does that chore say about the site?
opts: The soil is too fertile, and has to be moved on to poorer ground each year
The soil layer is thin, and on that gradient nothing holds it in place
The vines are too young for their roots to be binding the slope together
The rock beneath is impermeable, so all the rain has to run across the top
exp: A slope steep enough to need terraces, winches or a rope loses its fine material to every downpour, and there was very little of it to start with. That is the real cost of the celebrated steep vineyards: the work is manual, the soil is thin, and what the rain takes has to be carried back up by hand.

q: Terraces of loose reddish-black slate shot through with quartz cover the hills inland from Tarragona. Which Catalan name goes with that ground?
exp: Llicorella is slate weathered into loose plates, and it holds so little water that vines drive roots several metres down through the cracks in search of it. Yields are tiny as a result, and the wines come out correspondingly dense.

q: Mudstone buried deep comes back to the surface as a rock that splits into plates, and buried deeper still as one banded with coarse crystals. Which process has done that?
opts: Volcanism, the cooling of molten rock once it reaches the surface
Metamorphism, the reworking of a rock by heat and pressure
Erosion, the wearing away of a rock by running water and wind
Sedimentation, the settling of fine particles through still water
exp: Heat and pressure recrystallise a rock without ever melting it, and the deeper it goes the coarser the crystals it comes back with. Mud is the usual starting point in wine country, though the same treatment works just as well on a granite. Rocks of this family come to the surface in the old worn-down mountain belts, and for a vine the name matters less than whether the rock is fractured enough for roots and water to get into it.

q: Look down a valley in the Douro, the Rhine country or inland Catalonia and the hard splitting rocks are always under the steepest ground. Why do the two go together?
opts: Hard rock resists erosion, so it stands as ridges while softer ground wears away
Growers plant those rocks only where machinery could never have reached anyway
Rain washes such rock downhill until it collects on the steepest sections
Slate and schist are formed on steep ground and nowhere else on the map
exp: A river cuts down through whatever lies in its path, and the resistant rock is left standing as the sides of the valley. The vineyards follow because the slope and the sun are what make such places worth farming at all, since nobody would take on that gradient for a lesser crop.

q: Pale, coarse and speckled with crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica large enough to see, and it crumbles into a gritty acid sand as it weathers. Which rock?
exp: Granite cooled slowly deep underground, and slow cooling is what let its crystals grow big enough to pick out by eye. The sand it weathers into holds very little water or nutrient and is acidic, so a grower on granite faces an entirely different set of problems from one on limestone.

q: A soil test on weathered granite comes back at pH 5.2, well below what a vine would prefer. Which material is spread to correct that?
exp: Lime raises pH, and on acid crystalline ground spreading it is a routine part of preparing a site before planting. The others either push the soil further the wrong way or address a different problem altogether, so reaching for one of them here would make matters worse rather than better.

q: Squeezed deeper and hotter than the rocks that merely split, an old rock has its pale and dark minerals separate out into visible bands. What is the banded rock called?
exp: Gneiss forms where a rock has been buried deep enough for its light and dark minerals to gather into separate layers without the rock ever melting, and that banding is the giveaway in the hand. It weathers into a poor, stony, free-draining soil holding almost no water, so vines on it root deep and crop lightly.

q: A hard glassy mineral survives when everything it grew beside has weathered away, and it ends up as white pebbles scattered across the rows. Which mineral is it?
exp: Quartz is chemically almost indestructible, so it outlasts the feldspar and mica around it and finishes as sand, gravel and loose pale stones. Most of the world's sand is quartz for exactly that reason, which is worth knowing before crediting a white pebble with anything exotic.
